cards.title: Polynomial resolution length from logarithmic clause space
cards.formal:
Does logarithmic clause space imply polynomial refutation length for every fixed input clause width in general resolution?

Precisely, for every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and real constant \(a>0\), do there exist constants \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), depending only on \(k,a\), such that every unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formula \(F\) satisfies
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad L(F)\le B\,N(F)^d?\]
Here \(N(F)=2+|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|\) is formula size, \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\) is the minimum number of clauses simultaneously retained in a resolution refutation, and \(L(F)\) is its minimum number of axiom downloads and inference steps. These two minima are taken independently over all general resolution refutations. The short refutation whose existence is requested has no space restriction.
cards.why: The question asks whether a resolution proof that can be checked with only logarithmically many retained clauses necessarily has a short certificate somewhere in the same proof system. Resolving it would sharpen the relation between proof memory and proof length beyond the known constant-space case, without conflating proof existence with an efficient search algorithm.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean variable takes values in \(\{0,1\}\). A literal is a variable or its negation, and a clause is a finite set of literals interpreted as their disjunction. Clauses contain no repeated literal and no complementary pair \(x,\neg x\). The empty clause \(\bot\) is false. A CNF formula is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction; it is unsatisfiable if no assignment to its variables makes every clause true. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals in every input clause. The fixed input-width parameter \(k\) does not bound clauses derived during a proof.

The variable universe for a proof is the finite set of variables occurring in \(F\). Renaming these variables has no cost. The size \(N(F)\) counts input clauses and literal occurrences, with the added constant two ensuring that its logarithm is positive. Input clauses are a set, so padding by duplicate clauses does not change the formula or its size. If a concrete binary encoding is needed, number the occurring variables consecutively, encode each literal by its index and sign, and list clauses with delimiters. For fixed \(k\), this encoding and the stated combinatorial size are polynomially related; the logarithmic-space versus polynomial-length question is invariant under this choice of size convention.

A resolution refutation is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal D_0,\ldots,\mathcal D_T\), each a set of clauses over the input variables. Initially \(\mathcal D_0=\varnothing\), and the final configuration contains \(\bot\). Each step performs exactly one of the following operations. It may download one input clause \(C\in F\) into memory, adding it to the current set. It may erase one currently retained clause. It may add a resolvent \(C\cup D\) from two currently retained premises \(C\cup\{x\}\) and \(D\cup\{\neg x\}\), where neither \(C\) nor \(D\) contains the pivot variable and the resolvent is non-tautological. It may also weaken a retained clause by adding literals, provided the result is a clause over the same variables. These are the ordinary syntactic resolution and weakening rules. Arbitrary semantic consequence is not an additional inference rule.

Premises must be present before an inference, and they remain present after it unless erased in subsequent steps. An inference adds its conclusion before any such erasure, so the temporary memory needed to hold the conclusion is counted. An erased clause must be downloaded or derived again before reuse. The input formula itself is available for downloads without occupying working memory. Resolution proofs may share intermediate results arbitrarily; neither the tree-like restriction nor the regularity restriction forbidding repeated pivots on a proof path is imposed. No extension variables, stronger proof rules, randomization or error are allowed.

For a refutation \(\pi\), define
\[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}|\mathcal D_t|,\]
and let \(L(\pi)\) be its number of axiom-download and inference steps, with repetitions counted. Erasures are not counted in length. One can instead count all steps without changing polynomial-length bounds, because useful erasures can be bounded by the number of additions. Clause space counts each stored clause as one object regardless of its width. It is different from total literal space \(\max_t\sum_{C\in\mathcal D_t}|C|\), from the number of distinct variables in memory, and from the number of stored bits.

For an unsatisfiable formula, resolution completeness guarantees that the following finite integer minima exist:
\[\operatorname{Sp}(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}\operatorname{Sp}(\pi),\qquad L(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}L(\pi).\]
The refutation attaining the first minimum may have very large length. The question is whether a possibly different refutation of polynomial length must nevertheless exist whenever that minimum space is logarithmic.

The full quantifier order is \(\forall k\ge1\;\forall a>0\;\exists B>0,d\ge1\;\forall F\). The exponent \(d\) may depend on the input-width bound and the constant multiplying the logarithm, but not on the individual formula or its size. The proposition does not demand one exponent uniform in all \(k,a\), a procedure finding the short proof, or a transformation that keeps the original space bound.

A negative answer means that for some fixed \(k\) and \(a>0\), no polynomial bounds the minimum length throughout this class: for every \(B>0\) and \(d\ge1\), some unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF \(F\) has \(\operatorname{Sp}(F)\le a\log_2 N(F)\) but \(L(F)>B N(F)^d\). Thus it must establish genuinely superpolynomial unrestricted resolution length despite the small-space refutation. Merely proving that all proofs which retain small space are long does not refute the proposition.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the quantified implication. A positive answer must establish a polynomial length bound for all promised formulas, with its dependence on fixed \(k,a\) explicit or provably existent. A negative answer must prove the stated logical negation against all polynomial length bounds, including unrestricted-space refutations. A quasipolynomial upper bound, a theorem for constant clause space only, a result for tree-like resolution only, or a simultaneous length–space tradeoff does not settle the target. The statement is an exact asymptotic proposition; additive numerical tolerance is inapplicable.

context_blocks.text: Resolution combines clauses to certify that a Boolean formula is inconsistent. Its proof length is a basic lower bound on the work needed by resolution-based proof search, while clause space records how many learned facts must be retained together.

The memory measure here treats a clause as one object even when it is long. This makes logarithmic clause space fundamentally different from logarithmic bit space of an ordinary machine computation; a small number of clauses may encode many bits.

For constant-width input CNFs, the known space-to-width relation and the width counting bound imply \(L(F)\le N(F)^{O(\operatorname{Sp}(F)+k)}\). In particular, constant clause space implies polynomial length, whereas logarithmic clause space gives only a quasipolynomial bound \(N(F)^{O(\log N(F))}\). The question asks whether that remaining gap can always be removed.

The reverse implication behaves differently: the survey documents families with short refutations but large minimum clause space. Those examples do not decide whether small clause space forces short refutations.

A simultaneous-resource question asks whether a single proof can be both short and economical in memory. This card asks only whether a short proof exists at all. A tradeoff forcing a memory-limited proof to be long is compatible with a polynomial proof that uses more memory.

The 2023 work organizes connections among clause space, other space measures and tree-like proof size, and leaves major simultaneous-resource questions open in its concluding section. Those developments supply recent structural context but are not a solution or a newly restated confirmation of the precise logarithmic-space implication in this card.

cards.title: Frege lower bounds from circuit hardness
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{Frege is not polynomially bounded}.\]
Precisely, assuming that some NP language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuit family, must it be true that for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every constant \(C\ge1\), there is a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\), in the fixed system below, has
\[|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+1)^k?\]
This asks for a conditional connection between two lower-bound statements. It does not separately require proving the circuit-hardness premise.
cards.why: General Boolean circuit lower bounds and Frege proof lower bounds are two major barriers in complexity theory. A positive implication would make progress on the former sufficient for the latter, even without an explicit hard-tautology construction. It would clarify whether these difficulties are formally linked or whether proof complexity requires an additional source of hardness.

cards.definitions:
A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary string \(y\), with \(|y|\le p(|x|)\), satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). A Boolean circuit has input bits, constants zero and one, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one output. Its size is its number of gates, and its depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The class P/poly consists of languages decided at each input length \(n\) by a circuit \(D_n\) of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\), for fixed \(C,k\). These circuits need not be produced by an algorithm: they may be chosen nonuniformly. Thus NP not contained in P/poly asserts that at least one NP language has no such circuit family.

Fix the following classical Hilbert presentation of Frege. Formulas are finite trees built from propositional variables \(p_0,p_1,\ldots\), negation \(\neg\), and implication \(\to\). Under a Boolean assignment, negation reverses the truth value and \(A\to B\) is false exactly when \(A\) is true and \(B\) false. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its finitely many variables. The axiom schemes, allowing arbitrary formulas \(A,B,D\), are
\[A\to(B\to A),\]
\[(A\to(B\to D))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to D)),\]
\[(\neg A\to\neg B)\to(B\to A).\]
The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each an instance of an axiom scheme or obtained by this rule; its last formula is the theorem proved. No extension axioms introducing a new variable as an abbreviation for a formula are allowed.

Choose a fixed uniquely parsable binary tree encoding with constant-length tags for connectives and binary, self-delimited variable indices. Let \(|\varphi|\) be its bit length. Encode a proof by its full sequence of formula strings, with line delimiters; let \(|\pi|\) be that total bit length. Identical subformulas are written out each time they occur, not stored as a shared circuit. Earlier proof lines may be reused in multiple inferences. Including explicit rule tags and premise indices changes these sizes by at most polynomial factors and does not affect polynomial boundedness. The source recalls that standard finite complete Frege presentations polynomially simulate one another, so fixing this presentation does not change its lower-bound question.

Frege is polynomially bounded if there exist \(C,k\) such that every tautology has at least one proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\). Its negation does not require a polynomial-time generator for the hard tautologies or a single explicit family: existence of arbitrarily hard tautologies with the displayed quantifiers suffices. Formula size, proof size and circuit-input length are different parameters and are not silently identified.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication or of its negation. A positive proof may use exactly the circuit-hardness premise, without assuming additional cryptographic hardness, a feasible-interpolation property of Frege, or a lower bound for another system. A proof of the negation must establish both NP not contained in P/poly and polynomial boundedness of the fixed Frege system. An oracle separation or an obstruction to one reduction technique is not itself a negation of the stated unrelativized implication.

cards.title: Simultaneous polynomial-length constant-space refutations
cards.formal: Is the following statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and every family \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\) of unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formulas of size polynomial in \(n\), if there is a constant \(s\) such that every \(F_n\) has a resolution refutation using at most \(s\) clauses simultaneously, then there are constants \(S\ge1\), \(C>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every \(F_n\) has a single resolution refutation \(\pi_n\) with \[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi_n)\le S\qquad\text{and}\qquad L(\pi_n)\le C(n+1)^d.\] The constants may depend on the family and on \(k,s\), but not on \(n\). In particular, the conclusion may use a larger constant space bound \(S\) than the original bound \(s\).
cards.why: Proof length measures how many lines a refutation generates, and clause space measures how many it must retain at once. The question asks whether a formula that is easy in each measure separately can be hard when both restrictions apply to the same proof. Its constant-space regime makes it a sharp structural question about resolution and the interpretation of proof-memory bounds.

cards.definitions: Variables are drawn from a countable set. A literal is a variable or its negation. A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and a CNF formula is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals per input clause; derived clauses have no width bound. Define the size of \(F\) to be \(\sum_{A\in F}(1+|A|)\). Polynomial size means that some \(a>0,b\in\mathbb N\), fixed for the family, satisfy this size bound \(\le a(n+1)^b\) for every \(n\). The parameter \(n\) indexes the family; it need not equal the number of variables. There is no computability or uniform generation requirement on the family. A proof is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_t\), each a finite set of clauses, starting at \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\). One step may add an input clause from \(F\); add the resolvent \(A\cup B\) when \(A\cup\{x\}\) and \(B\cup\{\neg x\}\) are both currently present, with \(x\) absent from \(A\) and \(\neg x\) absent from \(B\); add a weakening \(A\cup B\) when \(A\) is present and \(B\) is any finite clause; or erase one currently present clause. An inference adds its conclusion before any separate erasure, so premises and conclusion coexist in that configuration. The proof ends with the empty clause present. The clause space is \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_j|\mathcal C_j|\), counting input clauses only while they have been downloaded and retained. The length \(L(\pi)\) is the number of input-clause downloads and inference steps, including weakenings and rederivations, but excluding erasures. Erased clauses may be downloaded or derived again; their reappearance is charged again. There is no read-once, tree-like, regularity or restriction on reuse. Space counts clauses regardless of how many literals they contain: it is not total literal space, variable space, bit memory or width. Length counts proof lines as specified, not the bit cost of manipulating a long clause. The target concerns existence of proofs with the two simultaneous bounds, not an efficient algorithm that finds them.

cards.title: Separating levels of bounded arithmetic
cards.formal:
Are there integers \(i>j\ge1\) and a closed first-order arithmetic sentence \(\theta\) such that
\[T_2^i\vdash\theta\qquad\text{and}\qquad T_2^j\nvdash\theta?\]
The theory \(T_2^r\) is BASIC together with induction for every \(\Sigma_r^b\) formula in the language defined below. The question asks for a separation as sets of provable sentences, with no assumed separation of computational complexity classes and no additional oracle symbols. One pair of levels is enough; it need not be fixed in advance, and proving strictness at every pair is not required.
cards.why: These theories organize arithmetic reasoning by the logical complexity permitted in induction hypotheses. Showing that even two positive levels prove different sentences would establish an unconditional difference in the strength of those reasoning principles. It would clarify how computational complexity is reflected in provability, beyond the known conditional connections.

cards.definitions:

Here \(H\) and \(\ell\) are unary, \(+\), \(\cdot\), \(\#\) are binary, and \(\le\) is a binary predicate. Terms are the finite expressions formed from variables, these constants and these function symbols. Atomic formulas are equalities or inequalities between terms. The logical operations are negation, conjunction, disjunction and first-order universal/existential quantification; implication and equivalence abbreviate their usual Boolean expansions. The successor notation \(Sx\) abbreviates \(x+1\), \(2\) abbreviates \(1+1\), and \(2x\) means \(2\cdot x\).

The intended standard structure has domain \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), its usual addition, multiplication and order, \(H(x)=\lfloor x/2\rfloor\), \(\ell(0)=0\), \(\ell(x)=\lfloor\log_2 x\rfloor+1\) for \(x>0\), and \(x\#y=2^{\ell(x)\ell(y)}\). This interpretation explains the symbols; the theory's nonlogical axioms are exactly the following finite BASIC list and the specified induction scheme, rather than all sentences true in this standard structure. Every free variable in the following displays is universally quantified.

The order and successor axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a\le b\ \to\ a\le b+1,\qquad a\ne a+1,\qquad 0\le a,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ a+1\le b,\qquad a\ne0\ \to\ 2a\ne0,\\
a\le b\lor b\le a,\qquad (a\le b\land b\le a)\ \to\ a=b,\\
(a\le b\land b\le c)\ \to\ a\le c,\qquad a\le a+b,\\
(a\le b\land a\ne b)\ \to\ (2a+1\le2b\land 2a+1\ne2b).
\end{gathered}\]
The addition and multiplication axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
a+b=b+a,\qquad a+0=a,\qquad a+(b+1)=(a+b)+1,\\
(a+b)+c=a+(b+c),\qquad a+b\le a+c\ \to\ b\le c,\\
a\cdot0=0,\qquad a\cdot(b+1)=a\cdot b+a,\qquad a\cdot b=b\cdot a,\\
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c),\\
1\le a\ \to\ ((a\cdot b\le a\cdot c)\leftrightarrow(b\le c)).
\end{gathered}\]
The length, halving and smash axioms are
\[\begin{gathered}
\ell(0)=0,\qquad \ell(1)=1,\qquad a\le b\ \to\ \ell(a)\le\ell(b),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (\ell(2a)=\ell(a)+1\land\ell(2a+1)=\ell(a)+1),\\
\ell(a\#b)=\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)+1,\qquad 0\#a=1,\\
a\ne0\ \to\ (1\#(2a)=2(1\#a)\land1\#(2a+1)=2(1\#a)),\\
a\#b=b\#a,\qquad \ell(a)=\ell(b)\ \to\ a\#c=b\#c,\\
\ell(a)=\ell(b)+\ell(c)\ \to\ a\#d=(b\#d)\cdot(c\#d),\\
a\ne0\ \to\ \ell(a)=\ell(H(a))+1,\\
a=H(b)\ \leftrightarrow\ (2a=b\lor2a+1=b).
\end{gathered}\]
These are the 32 axioms in Krajíček's Definition 5.2.1, regrouped by operation, with \(H\) and \(\ell\) replacing the printed halving and length notation. No sequence function or oracle predicate is added.

For a term \(t\) not containing \(y\), write \(\exists y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\exists y(y\le t\land\psi)\), and \(\forall y\le t\,\psi\) for \(\forall y(y\le t\to\psi)\). These are bounded quantifiers. They are sharply bounded when the bound is explicitly \(\ell(t)\). The bound may contain other free variables. Let \(\Sigma_0^b=\Pi_0^b\) be all formulas built from atomic formulas using Boolean operations and only sharply bounded quantifiers. Recursively, \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b,\Pi_{r+1}^b\) are the smallest pair of classes satisfying: both contain \(\Sigma_r^b\cup\Pi_r^b\); both are closed under conjunction, disjunction and both sharply bounded quantifiers; \(\Sigma_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded existential quantification; \(\Pi_{r+1}^b\) is closed under bounded universal quantification; and negation sends either class into the other. These are the full formula classes, allowing sharply bounded quantifiers inside as well as outside the other quantifiers, rather than only a strict prenex fragment.

For a set \(T\) of closed axioms, \(T\vdash\theta\) means that the closed sentence \(\theta\) has a finite proof in classical first-order logic with equality from those axioms. Equivalently, every nonempty \(L\)-structure satisfying all axioms of \(T\) satisfies \(\theta\). This equivalence is first-order completeness; structures in this characterization are not restricted to the standard natural numbers. There is no bound on proof length. Equality of theories here means equality of their deductive closures in the same language.

The separating sentence may have unrestricted first-order quantifiers; no complexity or syntactic bound on that witness sentence is part of the target.

The indices, finite formulas and finite proofs in the question range over ordinary standard mathematical objects. The nonprovability claim is external: it means that no finite proof from the weaker theory exists, rather than asking the weaker theory itself to prove its inability. A countermodel for the weaker theory and the sentence is an equivalent way to certify that nonprovability. A positive answer must be unconditional in the usual mathematical metatheory; adding an unproved complexity assumption changes the requested statement.

A negative answer must establish equality of the deductive closures for every pair \(i>j\ge1\). cards.title: Unprovability of polynomial circuit upper bounds in \(S_2^1\)
cards.formal:
Is the following unconditional unprovability statement true?
\[\forall k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists\eta\ \forall c\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}:\qquad S_2^1\nvdash\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta].\]
Here \(\eta(x,y)\) must be a \(\Sigma_1^b\) formula for which \(S_2^1\) proves that every \(x\) has exactly one output \(y\). It therefore represents a polynomial-time function. The sentence \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\), defined below with explicit coding, asserts that the predicate “the output is nonzero” has exact Boolean circuits of description size at most \(c n^k\) on every positive input length \(n\).

For each fixed exponent, the same represented function must resist provability for every fixed coefficient. The question concerns what this formal theory can prove; it does not ask directly for a circuit lower bound in the standard natural numbers or for unprovability of all possible upper bounds for one fixed function.
cards.why: Circuit upper bounds assert that small nonuniform computations exist, even when no efficient method for finding them is supplied. This question asks whether a theory designed to formalize polynomial-time reasoning can certify fixed-polynomial circuit bounds for every polynomial-time predicate. A positive result would expose an unconditional limitation on the power of such proofs without requiring the corresponding unconditional circuit separation.

Copy gates are only a serialization convenience and can be removed; this is an ordinary bounded-fan-in Boolean model.

In the lower bits, counted from position zero at the least significant bit, gate \(i\in\{0,\ldots,g-1\}\) has its tag at positions \(iq,iq+1\), first predecessor in the next \(w\) bits, and second predecessor in the next \(w\) bits. The output index occupies the \(w\) bits starting at \(gq\). A valid encoding has both predecessors below \(n+2+i\) and output below \(n+g+2\). Denote these conditions by \(\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\). The description size charged in the sentence is \(\ell(C)+\ell(g)\); the input length is supplied separately. Thus the measure is a binary description length, not an unannounced change to an exact gate-count bound.

All bit and field operations in this description have the following fixed bounded-arithmetic expansion. For \(X\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{Field}(X,a,b,v)\) by the existence of \(z,t,u,r,s\), all at most \(X+(1\#X)+1\), such that
\[\begin{gathered}
z=1\#H(z),\quad \ell(z)=a+1,\quad t=1\#H(t),\quad \ell(t)=b+1,\\
X=uz+r,\quad r<z,\quad u=st+v,\quad v<t.
\end{gathered}\]
Here \(a\) is the starting position, \(b\ge1\) is field width, and \(u< v\) abbreviates \(u\le v\land u\ne v\). The equations select \(z=2^a\) and \(t=2^b\). Define \(\operatorname{Bit}(X,a,e)\), for \(e\in\{0,1\}\), as
\[(\ell(X)\le a\land e=0)\ \lor\ (a<\ell(X)\land\operatorname{Field}(X,a,1,e)).\]
This also defines the padded zero bits of \(X=0\). In \(\operatorname{Valid}\), each extracted tag or index is a bounded existential variable at most \(n+g+4\); gate checks are quantified over \(i<g\). These conventions expand validity into one definite arithmetic formula.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\) to assert that the encoded circuit outputs one on the \(n\)-bit, zero-padded representation of \(x\). Its arithmetic expansion is: validity holds and there exists an integer
\[V\le (N\#N)\cdot(C\#C)\]
whose bits at node indices give a correct evaluation, with output bit one. Bits zero and one of \(V\) equal zero and one respectively; for each \(r<n\), bit \(r+2\) of \(V\) equals bit \(r\) of \(x\); and for each \(i<g\), the bit at \(n+2+i\) is the Boolean operation indicated by the tag applied to the predecessor bits. All field and bit occurrences use the preceding formulas, with Boolean auxiliary variables bounded by one and extracted indices bounded by \(n+g+4\). The four Boolean operations are specified by their truth tables. The output index is extracted from its field and its \(V\)-bit must be one. The quantifiers over nodes and gates are bounded by \(n\) and \(g\). Since validity implies \(g\le\ell(C)\) and \(n=\ell(N)\ge1\), the displayed bound is ample for the finite evaluation vector. This description fixes the formula through bounded quantifiers and Boolean combinations, and introduces no extra axioms about an opaque evaluator.

For fixed positive integers \(c,k\), let \(\operatorname{UB}_{c,k}[\eta]\) be the following closed \(L\)-sentence, with the defined predicates expanded:
\[\begin{split}
\forall N\ge1\ \exists g\ \exists C\ \bigl(&\operatorname{Valid}(n,g,C)\land\ell(C)+\ell(g)\le c\,n^k\\
&\land\forall x\ \forall y\bigl((\ell(x)\le n\land\eta(x,y))\to
(\operatorname{Eval}(N,n,g,C,x)\leftrightarrow y\ne0)\bigr)\bigr),
\end{split}\]
where every \(n\) abbreviates \(\ell(N)\). The fixed numeral \(c\) and fixed power \(n^k\) are expanded using multiplication. This is the source's Log convention: lengths come from the length of an arbitrarily quantified number, instead of treating their unary encodings as separately available objects. Zero input length is omitted. The quantifier \(\ell(x)\le n\) permits leading-zero padding; the represented function is a function of the number \(x\), exactly as in the source's unary function-symbol formulation.

The choices of \(k\), \(\eta\) and \(c\) in the main question are external standard integers/formulas. For each fixed exponent, one formula must work against every coefficient. The required conclusion is absence of any finite proof of each displayed upper-bound sentence, not that the theory proves its negation. The description encoding above makes a routine circuit serialization explicit; it is not a claim that the source printed this exact bit layout. Polynomially related standard circuit encodings yield the same all-exponents unprovability target after a fixed change of exponent and coefficient. No single EXP language or unproved complexity assumption substitutes for a provably total polynomial-time graph.

cards.definitions:
The theory is one-sorted classical first-order arithmetic with equality. We use Jeřábek's explicit presentation of \(PV_1\), cited as an alternative axiomatization by the source survey. Its base language is
\[
L=\{0,S,+,\cdot,\le,\#,\operatorname{len},M\}.
\]
In the intended structure on the nonnegative integers, \(S(x)=x+1\), \(\operatorname{len}(x)=\lceil\log_2(x+1)\rceil\), \(M(x,y)=\lfloor x/2^y\rfloor\), and \(x\#y=2^{\operatorname{len}(x)\operatorname{len}(y)}\). In particular \(\operatorname{len}(0)=0\). Write \(1=S(0)\), \(2=S(S(0))\), \(H(x)=M(x,1)\), and \(x<y\) for \(x\le y\land x\ne y\). These intended interpretations do not supply additional axioms.

The base theory has the universal closures of the following arithmetic axioms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x+0&=x,& x+S(y)&=S(x+y),\\
x\cdot0&=0,&x\cdot S(y)&=x\cdot y+x,\\
0&\le x,& S(y)\le x&\ \longleftrightarrow\ y<x,\\
M(x,0)&=x,&
M(x,y)&=2M(x,S(y))\ \lor\ M(x,y)=S(2M(x,S(y))),\\
\operatorname{len}(0)&=0,&
x\ne0&\ \longrightarrow\ \operatorname{len}(x)=S(\operatorname{len}(H(x))),\\
0\#1&=1,&
x\ne0&\ \longrightarrow\
\bigl(x\#1=2(H(x)\#1)\ \land\
y\#x=(y\#1)(y\#H(x))\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
It also has ordinary induction
\[
[A(0,\vec z)\land\forall x(A(x,\vec z)\to A(S(x),\vec z))]
\to\forall x\,A(x,\vec z)
\]
for every base-language formula \(A\) all of whose quantifiers are sharply bounded. A sharply bounded quantifier is \(\forall v\le\operatorname{len}(t)\) or \(\exists v\le\operatorname{len}(t)\), where \(t\) has no free occurrence of \(v\). A bounded universal quantifier expands to an implication, and a bounded existential quantifier to a conjunction. All induction parameters \(\vec z\) are universally closed.

Generate \(L_{PV}\) syntactically from \(L\) by finitely iterating two rules. For every existing term \(t\) with free variables among \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\), add an \(r\)-ary symbol \(f_t\). For every tuple of existing symbols \(g(\vec x),h_0(\vec x,y,z),h_1(\vec x,y,z),b(\vec x,y)\), add a new symbol \(R_{g,h_0,h_1,b}(\vec x,y)\). Arity is finite, the parameter tuple may be empty, and distinct construction trees are distinct symbols even when their intended functions agree. Include the universal closure of \(f_t(\vec x)=t(\vec x)\). For each recursion symbol, abbreviating it by \(R\), include exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(\vec x,y)&\le b(\vec x,y),\\
g(\vec x)\le b(\vec x,0)&\to R(\vec x,0)=g(\vec x),\\
y\ne0\land h_0(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y))\le b(\vec x,2y)
&\to R(\vec x,2y)=h_0(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y)),\\
h_1(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y))\le b(\vec x,S(2y))
&\to R(\vec x,S(2y))=h_1(\vec x,y,R(\vec x,y)).
\end{aligned}
\]
These are bounded-recursion constraints; no unconditional recursion equation is added when its bounding test fails.

Finally include polynomial induction
\[
[A(0,\vec z)\land\forall x(A(H(x),\vec z)\to A(x,\vec z))]
\to\forall x\,A(x,\vec z)
\]
for every quantifier-free \(L_{PV}\)-formula \(A\). Together with the base theory and the symbol axioms, these schemes define \(PV_1\) here. A proof is a finite derivation in classical first-order logic with equality from finitely many instances of these schemes. No true-universal arithmetic sentences, consistency assumptions, or external correctness axioms are added. The outer quantifier over unary symbols \(g\) ranges over their finite syntactic construction trees, not over an oracle for deciding which arbitrary programs run in polynomial time.

The SAT relation is fixed arithmetically, rather than by selecting an unspecified polynomial-time evaluator symbol. All abbreviations in this paragraph and below expand into formulas of the base language \(L\). Set \(\ell=\operatorname{len}(F)\), and define
\[
\operatorname{Bit}(x,i)\ \longleftrightarrow\
M(x,i)=2M(x,S(i))+1.
\]
Every auxiliary quantifier over a node, field, index or width is bounded by \(\ell\), with any smaller displayed bound imposed as a guard. Thus these quantifiers are sharply bounded. The one truth-table witness below has a separate bound.

The natural number \(F\) encodes an ordinary propositional formula tree whose nodes are numbered \(0,\ldots,m-1\), with children before their parents. Its variables are \(x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}\), with unused variables allowed. To define \(\operatorname{Form}(F,w,d,m)\), require \(w,d,m\le\ell\), \(w\ge2\), \(m\ge1\), \(w+d=\ell\), and
\[
\ell=w+2+(1+3m)w.
\]
The least significant \(w\) bits of \(F\) are all one and bit \(w\) is zero. Starting at bit \(w+1\) are \(1+3m\) fields of \(w\) bits, followed by the high sentinel bit one; the exact bit-length equality enforces that sentinel and forbids further bits. Put \(P=M(1\#F,d)\), whose intended value is \(2^w\). Field \(j\) has value \(r\) exactly when
\[
D(F,w,d,j,r)\ \longleftrightarrow\
r<P\ \land\
M(F,w+1+jw)=P\,M(F,w+1+(j+1)w)+r.
\]
Require field zero to have value \(m\). For each node \(i<m\), its fields \(1+3i,2+3i,3+3i\) have values \(\tau_i,u_i,v_i\), respectively. This notation abbreviates existentially quantified numbers at most \(\ell\) satisfying their three \(D\) relations, not new function symbols. Every record must satisfy exactly the relevant one of these four cases:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\tau_i & \text{record restrictions} & \text{meaning}\\
0 & u_i<m,\ v_i=0 & x_{u_i}\\
1 & u_i<i,\ v_i=0 & \neg\text{ child }u_i\\
2 & u_i<i,\ v_i<i & \text{child }u_i\land\text{child }v_i\\
3 & u_i<i,\ v_i<i & \text{child }u_i\lor\text{child }v_i .
\end{array}
\]
Every node \(i\) with \(S(i)<m\) must occur in exactly one child slot of all records, and the node \(r\) with \(S(r)=m\) in no child slot. Specifically, slot \((j,0)\) contains \(i\) when \(j<m,\tau_j\in\{1,2,3\},u_j=i\); slot \((j,1)\) contains \(i\) when \(j<m,\tau_j\in\{2,3\},v_j=i\). Denote this relation by \(C(j,s,i)\), with other slot values false. Exactly one means
\[
\exists j,s\le\ell\
[C(j,s,i)\land
\forall k,t\le\ell\,(C(k,t,i)\to(k=j\land t=s))].
\]
Together the record restrictions, field conditions and child-slot conditions define \(\operatorname{Form}\). In particular this encodes a tree, with no shared subtrees or circuit gates.

Define \(\operatorname{Eval}(F,a,v,w,d,m)\) by requiring, at every node \(i<m\), the following biconditional for the indicated record type:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\tau_i & \operatorname{Bit}(v,i)\text{ is equivalent to}\\
0 & \operatorname{Bit}(a,u_i)\\
1 & \neg\operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\\
2 & \operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\land\operatorname{Bit}(v,v_i)\\
3 & \operatorname{Bit}(v,u_i)\lor\operatorname{Bit}(v,v_i).
\end{array}
\]
Here \(v\) is the numeric table witness and \(v_i\) the second child field; their names designate different bound variables when the abbreviations are expanded. Now set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\ \longleftrightarrow\
\exists w,d,m,e\le\ell\ \exists v<1\#F\
[&\operatorname{Form}(F,w,d,m)\land e+m=\ell\\
 &\land a<M(1\#F,e)
 \land\operatorname{Eval}(F,a,v,w,d,m)\\
 &\land\exists r\le\ell\,(S(r)=m\land\operatorname{Bit}(v,r))].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(a\) is an assignment of \(m\) bits, allowing leading zeroes, and the first \(m\) bits of \(v\) are the values of the formula nodes with true root. The bound \(1\#F\) is \(2^\ell\), so the table has only linearly many bits in the input bit length. Malformed formula codes make \(\operatorname{Sat}\) false. No unrestricted exponentiation symbol or semantic SAT predicate is added to the theory.

For each syntactically generated unary symbol \(g\), let
\[
\Phi_g=\forall F\,\forall a\,
(\operatorname{Sat}(F,a)\to\operatorname{Sat}(F,g(F))).
\]
It asserts search correctness on every satisfiable formula. It imposes no required output on an unsatisfiable formula. The claim concerns absence of finite \(PV_1\) proofs of these sentences, not absence of semantically correct polynomial-time solvers as a separate assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that no generated unary symbol has a finite first-order derivation of its displayed SAT-search correctness sentence from the stated PV1 axioms, or a complete Lean proof of the negation, exhibiting a particular symbol and a valid finite derivation. The formalization must implement the stated syntactic theory and arithmetic SAT relation; any substitute SAT encoding or axiomatization must be proved to preserve the relevant provability claim. Neither assuming P differs from NP, adding all true universal arithmetic axioms, checking finitely many proofs, nor proving only a conditional statement settles this target.

The table relation is provably equivalent in the stated theory to the usual polynomial-time verifier; this is a concrete encoding convention for the source schema, not a change to its computational target.

The February 2026 paper formalizes probabilistic reasoning and proves a parity lower bound for constant-depth circuits inside the base theory. That result concerns a restricted computational model and does not show that the theory cannot prove the correctness of any polynomial-time SAT solver.

cards.definitions: Targets are Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) computed by finite acyclic fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT circuits with constants and one output. The target description explicitly lists gates and wire indices; its binary length is at most a supplied bound \(s\). A single oracle Turing machine \(A\) receives \(1^n,1^s\) and binary rationals \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), and may query \(f(x)\) at any chosen \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Queries may be adaptive and cost the time to write the query plus one step for the answer. The learner has independent fair random coins and no advice, target description or additional oracle. It outputs an explicit deterministic Boolean circuit \(H\) over the same basis. For every permitted input and target it must satisfy \(\Pr_{A\text{ coins}}[2^{-n}|\{x:H(x)\ne f(x)\}|\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\). There is one fixed polynomial \(p\) bounding its time, queries and output length on every random tape by \(p(n+s+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)+\operatorname{len}(\delta))\). The hypothesis need not lie within the target’s size bound; its encoding must obey this output bound. The quantifiers range over every \(n,s\ge1\) and every function with a target description of size at most \(s\). P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. NP consists of languages with polynomial-length witnesses checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Equality concerns languages on all binary inputs, not promise classes. The conclusion is deterministic P equals NP even though the learner is randomized. The implication allows arbitrary proofs and use of the fixed learner code; it is not restricted to black-box reductions.

cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has certificates of length polynomial in the string length that a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier can check.

A Cook–Reckhow proof system for \(L\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad \operatorname{range}(f)=L.\]
The input \(\pi\) is a proof and \(f(\pi)\) is the statement it proves. Thus every output is in \(L\), and every member of \(L\) has some proof. The running time is polynomial in \(|\pi|\), including writing the output. No polynomial bound in the statement length is imposed on the shortest proof. The system is one uniform algorithm, with no nonuniform advice.

For two systems \(f,g\) for the same language, \(f\) simulates \(g\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[\forall \pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists \sigma\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad f(\sigma)=g(\pi),\quad |\sigma|\leq p(|\pi|).\]
The polynomial may depend on the two systems, but not on the individual proof. The system \(f\) is optimal if it simulates every total polynomial-time system \(g\) whose range is exactly \(L\).

Only the existence of these short translated proofs is required. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm that computes \(\sigma\) from \(\pi\) defines the stronger notion of \(p\)-optimality, which is not the target here. Optimality also does not say that all statements have polynomial-length proofs: the comparison is against competing proof systems, not directly against statement length.

This card selects the existential question explicitly stated on page 2 of the source, making its broad page-3 discussion concrete. It asks for at least one language outside \(\mathrm{NP}\), without requiring arbitrarily high complexity or choosing the tautology language in advance. cards.definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.

cards.title: Li–Li conjecture
cards.formal:
For every network instance \(I\) defined below, is
\[\mathcal C(I)=\mathcal R(I)?\]
Here \(\mathcal C(I)\) is the closure of the rate vectors supported by finite deterministic causal zero-error network codes, with an entropy capacity shared between the two directions of every undirected edge. The region \(\mathcal R(I)\) consists of all rates supported by fractional multicommodity routing. The quantification includes every finite network size, every positive rational capacity vector, every finite list of independent unicast sessions, every finite message and symbol alphabet, every causal schedule and every nonlinear local encoding function.
cards.definitions:
Network and sessions. An instance is \(I=(G,c,((s_i,t_i))_{i=1}^k)\). The supply graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, connected, simple and undirected, with at least two vertices; an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Each edge \(e\) has a capacity \(c_e\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). The number of sessions \(k\) is a positive integer, and \(s_i,t_i\in V\) with \(s_i\ne t_i\). Different sessions may share either endpoint, have opposite directions, or have the same ordered endpoint pair. Such sessions still carry independent messages, each required at its own single destination.

Messages and initial knowledge. Choose a nonempty finite alphabet \(A_i\) for each session. The random variables \(M_i\) are independent and uniformly distributed on \(A_i\); singleton alphabets are allowed. Initially, a vertex \(v\) knows exactly the tuple of messages with \(s_i=v\), along with the fixed instance and code. Thus a destination can also know messages of other sessions for which it is itself a source. There is no additional message-dependent initial information and no private or shared random seed. Local computation and storage have no resource bound.

Causal finite code. Before messages are sampled, fix a nonnegative integer \(L\), a schedule \((u_\ell,v_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L\) with \(\{u_\ell,v_\ell\}\in E\), and nonempty finite transmitted-symbol alphabets \(\Sigma_\ell\). At step \(\ell\), the sender \(u_\ell\) sends \(Z_\ell\in\Sigma_\ell\) to \(v_\ell\). Its encoding function is an arbitrary deterministic function of all messages initially at \(u_\ell\) and the tuple of symbols received there at steps strictly less than \(\ell\). Previously sent symbols are already functions of that information. The schedule and alphabets do not depend on the messages; timing and unrecorded silence carry no extra information. For each \(i\), a deterministic decoder at \(t_i\), applied to its initially known messages and all symbols received there, must output \(M_i\) for every tuple in \(\prod_{j=1}^k A_j\). This is exact recovery with zero error. Linear encoding is not required.

Entropy and supported rates. All probabilities come from the uniform product distribution of the messages. For a finite random variable \(Z\), write
\[H(Z)=-\sum_{z:\Pr[Z=z]>0}\Pr[Z=z]\log_2\Pr[Z=z].\]
Entropy is measured in bits, so \(H(M_i)=\log_2|A_i|\). For each orientation \(u\to v\) of an edge, let \(X_{u\to v}\) be the ordered tuple of all symbols sent in that direction during the whole schedule; the empty tuple has entropy zero. For a real scale \(b>0\), a code supports \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) if
\[H(M_i)\ge b r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad H(X_{u\to v})+H(X_{v\to u})\le b c_{\{u,v\}}\quad(\{u,v\}\in E).\]
Each directional transcript is measured jointly across its uses, and the two directional entropies are then added. This is not the entropy of their combined bidirectional tuple, nor a separate full-capacity allowance in each direction. The positive scale normalizes messages and edge budgets together. It may depend on the code and need not be an integer. No bound on the schedule length or on the alphabets is imposed in terms of this scale.

Coding region. Let \(\mathcal C_0(I)\) be the set of supported rate vectors over all such finite codes, alphabets and positive scales, and let \(\mathcal C(I)=\overline{\mathcal C_0(I)}\) in the ordinary topology of \(\mathbb R^k\). Explicitly, \(r\in\mathcal C(I)\) means \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) and, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is \(r'\in\mathcal C_0(I)\) with \(\max_i|r_i-r'_i|<\varepsilon\). The closure allows limiting rates; it does not allow decoding errors. This card fixes the inherited entropy-capacity model. Equivalence with a fixed-length bit-budget or vanishing-error definition is not assumed.

Routing region. Let \(\mathcal P_i\) be the finite set of simple paths from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\) in \(G\). A vector \(r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^k\) belongs to \(\mathcal R(I)\) exactly when there are real numbers \(f_{i,P}\ge0\), one for every \(i\) and \(P\in\mathcal P_i\), such that
\[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_i}f_{i,P}\ge r_i\quad(1\le i\le k),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\sum_{\substack{P\in\mathcal P_i\\e\in P}}f_{i,P}\le c_e\quad(e\in E).\]
A unit of flow consumes one unit of capacity on every edge of its path, regardless of the traversal direction. Each commodity may split among arbitrarily many of these paths. Flows need not be integral. The region is a closed bounded polytope, since the graph, path lists and capacities are finite and every source differs from its destination. Multicast delivery of one common message to several receivers and recovery of functions instead of messages are different tasks.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal equality or its negation. An affirmative proof must cover all the specified instances, independent finite messages, deterministic causal nonlinear codes and positive scales, and must justify passage to the closure. The familiar inclusion \(\mathcal R(I)\subseteq\mathcal C(I)\) is also part of the checked equality; the substantive conjecture is the reverse inclusion.

A negative answer may give one finite instance, a finite code, a positive scale and a supported rate vector outside \(\mathcal R(I)\). The checked proof must establish every encoder's causality, exact decoding on every message tuple, the transcript-entropy capacity inequalities, and infeasibility of the fractional routing constraints at that rate. This finite-code form loses no possible counterexample: a point of the coding closure outside the closed routing region has a neighborhood disjoint from that region and hence contains a supported finite-code rate.

Beating a particular routing algorithm, integral paths, or a cut bound does not establish a separation from the optimal fractional region. A result for directed edges, correlated messages or multicast does not refute this statement. An impossibility result only for linear encoders does not prove it. Any use of a different error or capacity convention requires a checked implication to the model above. There is no additive numerical tolerance on this exact yes-or-no equality.

context_blocks.text: Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits \(x\) and \(y\), it may send \(x\oplus y\); a receiver that already knows \(y\) can recover \(x\). Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match coding for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide necessary information bounds, but meeting all of them need not make multiple demands fractionally routable. In the unit-capacity \(K_{3,2}\) example, put vertices \(a,b,c\) on one side and \(d,e\) on the other, and use sessions \((a,b),(b,c),(c,a),(d,e)\) at one common rate. The sparsity bound is one, while the maximum concurrent routing rate is \(3/4\). Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval prove that coding also cannot exceed \(3/4\). Thus a cut–flow gap alone is not a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family whose gap grows as a positive power of \(\log |V|\). General cut–flow bounds give a logarithmic upper bound. Consequently a single strict separation would imply unbounded asymptotic improvements, rather than merely an isolated constant-factor gain.

Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that the conjecture implies an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for Boolean circuits multiplying two \(n\)-bit integers when both fan-in and fan-out are bounded by a constant. Their theorem is conditional on the network-coding conjecture; a multiplication lower bound has not already been obtained from ordinary cut constraints. The bounded-degree circuit model matters to the stated consequence.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. cards.context:
Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits \(x\) and \(y\), it may send \(x\oplus y\); a receiver that already knows \(y\) can recover \(x\). Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match coding for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide necessary information bounds, but meeting all of them need not make multiple demands fractionally routable. In the unit-capacity \(K_{3,2}\) example, put vertices \(a,b,c\) on one side and \(d,e\) on the other, and use sessions \((a,b),(b,c),(c,a),(d,e)\) at one common rate. The sparsity bound is one, while the maximum concurrent routing rate is \(3/4\). Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval prove that coding also cannot exceed \(3/4\). Thus a cut–flow gap alone is not a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family whose gap grows as a positive power of \(\log |V|\). General cut–flow bounds give a logarithmic upper bound. Consequently a single strict separation would imply unbounded asymptotic improvements, rather than merely an isolated constant-factor gain.

Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that the conjecture implies an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for Boolean circuits multiplying two \(n\)-bit integers when both fan-in and fan-out are bounded by a constant. Their theorem is conditional on the network-coding conjecture; a multiplication lower bound has not already been obtained from ordinary cut constraints. The bounded-degree circuit model matters to the stated consequence.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.
